'''Walter Eric Spear''' (20 January 1921 – 21 February 2008)<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Adams | first1 = A. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2009.2003 | title = Walter Eric Spear. 20 January 1921 -- 21 February 2008 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 55 | pages = 267–289 | year = 2009 | doi-access = free }}</ref> was a German physicist whose work helped develop large area electronics and thin film displays.<ref name="rse">{{cite web|url=https://www.rse.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/obits_alpha/spear_w.pdf|title=Walter Eric Spear|work=Obituary|publisher=[[The Royal Society of Edinburgh]]|author=Alexander G Fitzgerald|access-date=3 August 2018}}</ref> He was born in Frankfurt to a Jewish father and a Lutheran mother; by the time he finished his school examinations in 1938, life for Jews and people associated with Jews was becoming difficult.  With the support of friends and relatives in Britain, the family moved to London where he arrived in 1938 "with a small suitcase and a large cello".<ref name="rse"/><ref name=WESlautEAD>{{cite journal | doi=10.1002/pssc.200982906| title=Walter E Spear: A Tribute| journal=Physica Status Solidi C| volume=7 |issue=3–4 | pages=501–504| year=2010| last1=Davis| first1=E. A.| bibcode=2010PSSCR...7..501D}}</ref>

==Education==
Wanting to pursue a scientific career, Spear attended evening classes for the University of London entrance examination, which he passed before the family [[Defence Regulation 18B#Expansion in May 1940|were interned]] on the [[Isle of Man]] as suspected [[Axis powers|Axis]] sympathisers. They were soon released, and Spear joined the [[Royal Pioneer Corps]] in 1940, later moving to the [[Royal Artillery]] where he became a Bombardier before being demobilized in 1946.<ref name="rse" />

==Career==
Spear graduated in 1950 and obtained a Research Fellowship that allowed him to stay there to do additional work. He left [[Birkbeck, University of London|Birkbeck]] in 1953 to take up a position at [[University College, Leicester]], where he did research on amorphous selenium films.<ref name="rse" />

One of his PhD students at Leicester was [[Alf Adams]],<ref name="BBC R4"/> the British physicist who invented the [[strained-layer quantum-well laser]]. Spear left Leicester in 1968 after being offered the Harris Chair of Physics at the [[University of Dundee]].

It was while working at Leicester that Spear first came into contact with a student named [[Peter LeComber]],<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Spear | first1 = W. E. | author-link1 = Walter Eric Spear| doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1994.0013 | doi-access = free| title = Peter George Lecomber. 19 February 1941 – 9 September 1992 | journal = Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society | volume = 39 | pages = 214–226 | year = 1994 }}</ref> with whom he would work closely throughout his career. LeComber went with Spear to Dundee, and together they became known for their joint research into the properties of [[amorphous silicon]].<ref name="Notable University Figures">{{cite web|title =Notable University Figures (2) Professor Walter E. Spear|url=http://www.archives-records-artefacts.blogspot.com/2011/07/notable-university-figures-2-professor.html|publisher=Archives, Records and Artefacts at the University of Dundee|access-date=11 August 2011|date=29 July 2011}}</ref>

The work carried out by Spear and LeComber and their research team in this field led to the creation of the amorphous film silicon transistor, which led to [[LCD]] technology and to the eventual development of technologies such as flat screen TVs and [[solar panels]].<ref name="Notable University Figures" /> While at Dundee they also established the Amorphous Materials Research Group, which was devoted to the study of non-crystalline solids.<ref name=Museum>{{cite web|title=Physics Collection Key Figures|url=http://www.dundee.ac.uk/museum/collections/physics/keyfigs.htm|publisher=University of Dundee|access-date=11 August 2011|archive-date=24 September 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120924095130/http://www.dundee.ac.uk/museum/collections/physics/keyfigs.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

When Spear retired in 1988, he was succeeded in the Harris Chair by LeComber, who died in 1992.<ref name="Notable University Figures" />

==Awards and honours==
In 1972 Spear was made a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]], in 1976 he was awarded the [[Europhysics Prize]], and in 1977 the Max Born Medal by the [[Institute of Physics]].<ref name="rse" /> In 1980 he was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of London]] and awarded the [[Makdougall Brisbane Prize]] of the Royal Society of Edinburgh.<ref>{{Cite web| url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/obits_alpha/spear_w.pdf | title=Walter Eric Spear | access-date=22 July 2016 | archive-date=12 August 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160812185210/https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/obits_alpha/spear_w.pdf | url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1988 he was awarded the Rank Prize, and the same year presented the Royal Society [[Bakerian Lecture]]. In 1990 he was awarded their [[Rumford Medal]], and he retired soon afterwards.<ref name="rse" /> His nomination for the Royal Society reads {{centered pull quote|Professor Spear is distinguished for his experimental research over a period of nearly two decades on electronic transport in condensed matter, particularly measurements of the drift mobility. His work was the first to establish an activated mobility of polaron type in a molecular crystal (sulphur), and a mobility edge in a non-crystalline material (glow discharge deposited silicon). He has determined the density of states in the gap in this material by field effect measurements and their role in [[photoconductivity]], and has recently shown that, contrary to previous ideas, it can be doped. His work is characterised by high experimental skill, felicitous choice of materials and full theoretical understanding.<ref name="royal">{{Cite web | title=Spear, Walter Eric | url=https://www.webcitation.org/6ORWJVHJm?url=http://royalsociety.org/DServe/dserve.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo==%27EC%2F1980%2F34%27) | access-date=2025-08-22 | website=www.webcitation.org}}</ref>}}

Spear's archives are held by Archive Services, University of Dundee.<ref name="Notable University Figures" /><ref name=Arccat>{{cite web|title=UR-SF 57 Professor Walter E. Spear|url=http://arccat.dundee.ac.uk/dserve.exe?&dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=Show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo==%27UR-SF%2057%27)|website=Archive Services Online Catalogue|publisher=University of Dundee|access-date=16 June 2015}}</ref> As well as including academic works by Spear and notes for talks and lectures, they include Spear's ‘Scientific Curiosities and Absurdities’ file which features some of the more unusual correspondence Spear received.<ref name="Notable University Figures" /><ref name=Contact>{{cite journal|title=From the Archives: Professor Walter Spear's Scientific Curiosities and AbsurditiesProfessor Walter Spear's Scientific Curiosities and Absurdities|journal=Contact|date=February 2010|pages=21|url=http://www.dundee.ac.uk/pressoffice/contact/2010/feb2010.pdf|access-date=11 August 2011|archive-date=24 September 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120924095141/http://www.dundee.ac.uk/pressoffice/contact/2010/feb2010.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Personal ==
Spear's mother was a professional violinist and teacher. Spear inherited a 17h century Italian cello while a boy and received cello lessons from the age of 8. He was an amateur cellist throughout his life. His father, David Spear, was a graphic artist who later became a photographer.<ref name="rse"/>

Spear was survived by his widow, born Hilda D. King, whom he had married in Middlesex in 1952,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.freebmd.org.uk/cgi/information.pl?cite=Fo9jtNupF78Z92u6agoLoA&scan=1| title=Index entry|access-date=3 August 2018|work=FreeBMD|publisher=ONS}}</ref> by the couple's two daughters and their children.<ref name="rse"/>
